The Pale-tailed barbthroat (Threnetes leucurus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate of 27.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 27.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a value consistent with the elevated metabolic demands typical of small-bodied trochilids. Newly hatched chicks, emerging from the incubated bird egg after an incubation period maintained at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], display a remarkably low neonatal mass of just 0.86 grams [Wwb = 0.86 grams]. This modest weight at birth, recorded within the first day of the exotrophic transition, underscores the altricial condition of nestlings that are entirely dependent on parental provisioning. The incubation period itself, measured under controlled laboratory conditions, lasts approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days] at that same incubation temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], a duration that falls within the expected range for hummingbirds of comparable size. These early life-history traits collectively suggest a strategy favoring rapid embryonic development at the cost of producing extremely altricial, low-mass neonates that require intensive post-hatching care.

Significant sexual dimorphism in ultimate body mass is evident among adults of this species, with mature females attaining a maximum wet weight of 5.7 grams [Wwi = 5.7 grams] while males reach a notably larger ultimate wet weight of 6.5 grams [Wwi = 6.5 grams]. This difference, representing roughly a 14% disparity in mass, is likely linked to the divergent selective pressures associated with male-male competition for foraging territories, a common phenomenon among hermits. Under the thermal conditions typical of an actively foraging adult, with a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the progression through key developmental milestones follows a predictable schedule. The fledgling achieves its first flight achievement relatively early, at approximately 23 days after hatching [tx = approximately 23 days after hatching], marking the point of at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]nest departure. This rapid acquisition of flight capability is critical for escaping predation and beginning independent foraging in the dense understory of their Amazonian and Guianan forest habitats, although full nutritional independence from the provisioning adult is not achieved immediately.

Reproductive output in the Pale-tailed barbthroat is constrained by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting events. Females typically lay a clutch containing 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and under optimal conditions, they produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually]. This modest annual fecundity, which corresponds to an implicit daily reproduction rate of two eggs per 365 days, is characteristic of a slow life-history pace observed in many tropical insectivores and nectarivores. The timing of first reproduction occurs relatively late in life compared to temperate hummingbirds; the time since birth at first brood has been recorded as 365 days [tR = 365 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This extended period before initiating reproductive activity likely reflects the time required for a juvenile to secure a stable territory, complete somatic growth, and acquire the foraging proficiency necessary to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

The onset of sexual maturation, marking the point at which the immature individual becomes physiologically capable of breeding, occurs well before the actual first breeding event. Puberty in this species, as determined by gonadal development under favorable thermoregulatory conditions at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], is reached at approximately 69 days since birth [tp = approximately 69 days since birth]. This relatively early attainment of reproductive maturity compared to the delayed age at first reproduction suggests that social or ecological factors, such as competition for display sites or the need to accumulate sufficient fat reserves, impose a substantial lag between physiological readiness and actual breeding. The intervening period, spanning from 69 days to approximately one year of age, is likely spent in a non-breeding, subadult state, with young birds prospecting for territories and refining their foraging skills. This reproductive schedule contrasts sharply with that of some temperate hummingbirds, which may breed within their first year but often face a shorter window of resource abundance.

Longevity records for the Pale-tailed barbthroat indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] when considered under the typical active metabolic conditions at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lifespan is comparatively long for a bird of its diminutive size and places it among the longer-lived members of the Trochilidae. The slow pace of life suggested by the low annual fecundity, the late age at first reproduction, and the delayed interval between maturity and breeding is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high reproductive output. Such a strategy is common among tropical species that experience relatively low and seasonally predictable resource availability, where the probability of successfully rearing multiple broods across several years outweighs the benefits of investing heavily in a single season. The interplay between a modest metabolic rate, a small body size, and a relatively extended lifespan underscores the ecological specialization of this understory hermit.
